text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Swedish retail union Handels has agreed with the retail employers' association and leading retail companies to freeze current wage agreements --which give moderate pay rises -- until the year 2000. In a joint declaration the parties called on other sectors to follow suit in an attempt to give politicians room to fight unemployment without boosting inflation.

- Currently high Swedish share prices do not reflect the new business climate of no inflation and downward price pressure on products, Thomas Halvorsen, head of public pension fund Fourth AP says. Halvorsen is one of the largest fund managers on the Stockholm Stock Exchange with close to 70 billion crowns in his portfolio. The February CPI fell 0.4 percent year-on-year.

- The government's energy proposal, due to be presented on Friday, merely includes broad outlines and principles to get the necessary changes going when nuclear power plant Barseback closes. The minority Social Democrat government has decided to start phasing out nuclear power, starting with one of Barseback's two reactors in 1998 and the other later.

- The import of American hormone-treated calves' stomachs, which have been used by Swedish dairies for producing cheese, was abruptly stopped on Wednesday after Swedish public radio told listeners that the product was used to make more than a fifth of all rennet used in Swedish cheese.

- Swedish Minister of Industry and Commerce Anders Sundstrom does not have any strategy for reaching targeted levels of carbon dioxide emissions after the phasing out of nuclear power stations. He is appointing a commission of inquiry. T
- If GDP continues to grow at the 1996, fourth-quarter rate of 1.1 percent over the following three quarters it will give an annual growth rate of nearly 4.5 percent.

- The Swedish Financial Inspectorate reports that only 0.2 percent of Stockholm-listed shares were bought with money borrowed against other securities. The practice of borrowing heavily to speculate in stocks was one of the factors behind the banking and finance crash of the early 1990s.
- Former Volvo CEO Pehr Gyllenhammar has been invited to join the supervisory board at music and entertainment giant Polygram.

- Justice Minister Laila Freivalds has refused to speed up repeal of laws forbidding share buybacks. Cash-heavy firms will not be able to buy back their own shares before April 1, 1998, the ministry says. REUTER
